CONDITIONAL: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 4, audited at commit cf155e3 (committed; working tree carries only
sprint bookkeeping moves). Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict,
including both 16 Aug amendments (the re-scope away from auth, and R8's change from
"drop by migration" to "delete the file outright").

VERDICT: CONDITIONAL PASS. One required fix, in .github/workflows/ci.yml and one
sentence of README.md. The security thinking in this sprint is the best work I have
audited in this project; the gate it builds is wired one line short of actually
being a gate.

REQUIRED FIX -- the rls-tests job does not gate the migration it exists to protect,
and README claims it does.

.github/workflows/ci.yml adds `rls-tests` as a standalone job with no dependants.
`migrate` still declares only `needs: build`. So on a push to main where the RLS
suite goes red, `migrate` runs anyway: `supabase db push` applies the very migration
whose policies just failed their tests, to production, while the workflow shows red.
The suite is a notification, not a gate.

README.md then states the opposite, in the path-to-production list:

  "It fails the build the same way lint/typecheck/test do -- a change that weakens a
  policy never reaches `main` in the first place, rather than being caught after the
  fact against production."

Both halves of that sentence are wrong as written. A red check does not stop anything
reaching main -- that needs a branch protection rule, which is a GitHub setting and
is not (and cannot be) configured in this repository. And "rather than being caught
after the fact against production" is precisely backwards, because production is
exactly where a weakened policy lands today.

Fix:
  migrate:
    needs: [build, rls-tests]

and rewrite the README sentence to claim what the workflow will then actually
deliver: the suite fails the build, and a red suite blocks the migration from
reaching production. Not that it blocks the push.

I am requiring this rather than noting it because this sprint's entire thesis is
"RLS policies proven by test." A proof that does not block the deploy of the thing it
disproves is a weaker artifact than it looks, and the repository currently documents a
guarantee it does not implement. One line of YAML closes most of the gap. It also
makes note 1 below harmless, since a job that fails for any reason then stops the
migration instead of being ignored.

Requirements coverage:
R1/R2 MET, and the reasoning behind it is correct in a way I did not expect. There is
  no SELECT policy on readings at all -- retrieval by id is a security definer
  function, get_reading_by_id(uuid). The migration comment explains why, and it is
  right: RLS is a row predicate, it cannot see whether the caller's query carried a
  WHERE clause, so `using (true)` -- the obvious-looking way to write "readable by
  id" -- returns the whole table on an unfiltered select. That is the exact trap R1's
  acceptance criterion names as an automatic failure, and this diff not only avoids
  it but writes down why, so the next person does not "fix" the missing select policy.
  Insert is a real policy (to anon, with check (true)); update and delete are denied
  by having no policy at all. The only `true` in the file is on the insert policy's
  WITH CHECK, not a select condition.
R3 MET. readings.id is uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid() (Sprint 2's
  migration, still intact at cf155e3). v4, cryptographically random. Not sequential,
  not timestamp-derived. This matters more here than in any prior sprint: with auth
  cut, the id IS the access control, and the migration says so out loud.
R4 MET. All six listed cases are present as distinct tests with real assertions:
  cannot list, can retrieve a known id, random unguessed id returns nothing, can
  insert, cannot update, cannot delete. The update and delete tests correctly expect
  a successful zero-row operation rather than a thrown error -- that is what RLS
  actually does, and getting this wrong is the usual way these suites end up asserting
  nothing -- and both then re-read the row through the function to prove it is
  unchanged. That second half is what makes them real tests rather than assertions
  about error objects.
R5 MET. tables_without_rls() queries pg_class/pg_namespace, not a hardcoded list.
R6 MET as literally written -- the suite runs against a local stack started in CI and
  a failure fails the build -- but see the required fix for what "fails the build"
  does and does not currently buy. Note R6 has no QA1 acceptance criterion of its own
  in the sprint file; I audited it against the requirement text.
R7 MET, and I checked it as a direct grep the way the sprint asked. Zero references
  to the service role key anywhere under supabase/tests/, vitest.rls.config.ts,
  vitest.config.ts, .github/, or lib/supabase/config.ts. The suite builds its client
  from resolvePublicConfig(), which reads only NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and
  NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY. Repo-wide, the service role key survives only in
  lib/supabase/admin.ts and its test, which is Sprint 2's health route and correct.
  I also confirmed the suite cannot pass vacuously by being empty: `npm run test:rls`
  with no stack configured exits 1 with "Supabase client requires
  NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL...", so the file is genuinely collected rather than
  silently matching nothing.
R8 MET, against the amended requirement, and the amendment's reasoning checks out
  statically. No proxy.ts, no sign-in or account routes, no user_id in any migration,
  @supabase/ssr gone from package.json. I verified the claim the amendment rests on:
  origin/main is at 389040c and carries exactly two migrations, 20260815221042 and
  20260816125144. 20260816131120_add_user_id_to_readings.sql is on no remote, so
  deleting it outright writes no fiction into applied history and the forward-only
  rule is not violated. NOTE the sprint file contradicts itself here: R8's amended
  text says delete the file outright, while the QA1 acceptance criterion below it
  still says "user_id is removed by migration, not by editing an existing migration
  file." The criterion was not updated with the requirement. I audited against the
  amended requirement, since it is dated later and states its reasoning. Someone
  should reconcile the criterion so the next reader is not led to fail a correct diff.
R9 MET. README documents how to run the policy tests (npx supabase start, then
  npm run test:rls, with the reason they are excluded from npm run test) and what each
  class protects, including the insert-cannot-return-its-own-id consequence.

Verified by execution:
- lint, typecheck, default test suite: all exit 0, 8 tests across 3 files.
- vitest split works as intended: `npm run test` collects only lib/** (no attempt to
  reach a database), `npm run test:rls` collects only supabase/tests/**.
- next build exits 0. Route table is back to / static plus /api/health/db dynamic --

- Rebuilt with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="QA1PROBESERVICEROLE" and grepped all of

- The RLS policies themselves are NOT verified. No Docker on this machine, so no
  local stack, no PostgREST, no way to execute the suite. Dev Team flagged this same

  My review of the policies is a reading of Postgres RLS semantics, not a live test.

Notes, not conditions:
1. `supabase status -o env ... >> "$GITHUB_ENV"` is unverified, as the commit message
   says. The flags and override names match the CLI's own documented example (I
   checked `supabase status --help`), so that part is right. What I could not confirm
   without Docker is whether `-o env` emits shell-quoted values (KEY="value"). If it
   does, GITHUB_ENV takes the quotes as part of the value and the suite gets a
   malformed URL. Cheap defensive fix, correct either way:
     supabase status -o env --override-name ... | tr -d '"' >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
   Not a condition because it fails loudly on the first CI run rather than silently,
   and once the required fix lands, a failing rls-tests job stops the migration
   instead of being ignored.
2. tables_without_rls() is granted to anon, so it is callable by anyone on production
   forever, to serve a test. In the healthy case it returns an empty set and leaks
   nothing. In the unhealthy case it tells an attacker exactly which table lost its
   RLS. That is a direct consequence of R7 forbidding the service role key in the
   suite, so it is a requirement-driven tradeoff rather than a mistake -- but it is a
   permanent production API surface added for test convenience, and it should be a
   deliberate decision rather than an accident. If it ever needs closing, the answer
   is running the coverage check over a direct database connection in CI instead of
   the Data API.
3. tables_without_rls() filters `c.relkind = 'r'`, which is ordinary tables only. A
   partitioned table is relkind 'p' and would be invisible to the coverage check --
   the exact silent-gap failure R5 exists to prevent, just one relkind over. Widen it
   to `c.relkind in ('r','p')`.
4. In the "cannot update" test, `data?.[0].place_name` guards data being null but not
   the array being empty, so a genuinely deleted row throws a TypeError instead of
   failing the assertion cleanly. It fails either way, so this is cosmetic.
5. Carried forward and still true: the schema_migrations ledger depends on every
   migration remembering its own insert, enforced by nothing. This one remembered.

CONDITION -- rls-tests now gates the migration. FIXED, both halves.

  migrate:
    needs: [build, rls-tests]

Parsed the workflow and walked the job graph rather than eyeballing the diff:
  build      needs=None            if=None
  rls-tests  needs=None            if=None
  migrate    needs=[build,rls-tests]  if=github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'

That is the right shape. rls-tests carries no `if` of its own, so it always runs and
can never land in the skipped state that would let a `needs` dependant slip through
on a technicality. A red RLS suite now stops supabase db push from applying that
same migration to production, which is what this sprint's thesis required all along.

The README correction is the part I care about as much as the YAML. It now says the
gate blocks the migration from reaching production, and states plainly that it does
NOT stop code landing on main -- that would need branch protection configured on the
GitHub repository, which no workflow file can enforce on its own. That is accurate,
and it is a better sentence than the one it replaces because it tells the reader
where the remaining gap is instead of papering over it. Worth someone actually
configuring that branch protection at some point; it is outside this sprint and
outside this repository.

Scope: one file, .github/workflows/ci.yml, six lines including comment.

THE FIX. Correct, and confirmed by reality rather than by argument.

  | tr -d '"' >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

This is round 1's note 1, which I raised sight unseen because I had no Docker to
settle it and recommended the fix that would be right either way. CI settled it:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL arrived as the literal quoted string
"http://127.0.0.1:54321" and supabase-js's validateSupabaseUrl rejected it.
`-o env` quotes for shell sourcing; GITHUB_ENV's KEY=value parser does not strip.
The commit says so plainly instead of dressing it up, which is the right way to
record a confirmed hypothesis.

The blanket strip is safe for these two values specifically -- a URL and a
base64url JWT cannot legitimately contain a double quote -- and the comment in the
workflow says why, so nobody later widens it to a value where it would matter.

Re-verified at 3648d7a:
- .github/workflows/ci.yml parses as valid YAML; job graph unchanged and still

  never be skipped into letting a dependant through), migrate needs [build,
  rls-tests] gated to main + push. Round 2's condition is still in place.
- lint, typecheck, default test: exit 0, 8 tests across 3 files.
- `npm run test:rls` with no stack configured still exits 1 on

Notes, not conditions:
1. NEW, introduced by this fix: the step no longer fails when `supabase status`
   fails. GitHub Actions' default shell for `run:` on Linux is `bash -e {0}` --
   `-e`, but NOT `pipefail`. Before this commit the export was a simple command, so
   a non-zero `supabase status` failed the step. Now it is the left side of a pipe,
   so the step's exit status is `tr`'s, which is 0. Demonstrated rather than
   asserted:
     bash -e     -c 'false | tr -d "\"" > /dev/null'   -> exit 0   (step "succeeds")
     bash -eo pipefail -c 'false | tr -d "\"" > /dev/null' -> exit 1 (step fails)
     bash -e     -c 'false >> /dev/null'                -> exit 1  (the old behaviour)
   Fix is one line -- add `shell: bash` to the step (which gets you
   `--noprofile --norc -eo pipefail`), or `set -o pipefail` at the top of the run
   block.
   Not a condition because it cannot produce a green-and-wrong result: with no env
   exported, `npm run test:rls` throws on missing configuration and fails the job,
   which I re-verified above. What it costs is diagnosability -- the build still
   goes red, but it points at the test instead of at the export step that actually
   broke. Worth fixing next time this file is open.
2. `supabase status -o env` emits every status variable, not just the two that were
   renamed -- the local stack's SERVICE_ROLE_KEY among them -- and all of it now
   lands in the job environment. No harm today: these are the well-known local-stack
   values, not production secrets; the emitted name does not match the
   SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY that lib/supabase/admin.ts reads; and nothing under
   supabase/tests/ touches either. But R7 exists precisely to keep a service role
   key out of reach of this suite, and leaving one in ambient job env is the setup
   for a future test picking it up and passing vacuously. Tightening the export to
   `| grep -E '^NEXT_PUBLIC_'` would export exactly what is needed. Cheap, and it
   pairs naturally with note 1 since both are edits to the same three lines.
3. Carried forward unchanged: tables_without_rls() is anon-callable on production
   forever to serve a test (requirement-driven tradeoff, worth revisiting
   deliberately); its `relkind = 'r'` filter misses partitioned tables ('p'), which
   is R5's own silent-gap failure one relkind over; the sprint file still contradicts
   itself on R8 (amended requirement says delete the file outright, the acceptance
   criterion below still says "removed by migration"), which someone should reconcile
   so the next reader is not led to fail a correct diff; `data?.[0].place_name` in
   the update test throws rather than asserting cleanly on an empty array; the
   schema_migrations ledger convention remains enforced by nothing.

PASS: GroundTruth live test, Sprint 4, commit 3648d7aa3af3c490079a950d9ad19955bad0d6e2. Environment: production Data API at rzlojpwlhbcfzpohbwso.supabase.co, and https://my-little-racoon.vercel.app, 2026-08-16 ~15:15 UTC. Performed with the real production anon (publishable) key against production, as the sprint file requires -- NOT inferred from the CI suite passing. VERDICT: PASS. All three live criteria verified. Four findings recorded below; none of them fails a criterion, two of them will bite Sprint 10 if nobody reads this. PRECONDITIONS CONFIRMED FIRST - Deploy live at the shipped commit: page renders 3648d7a, matching origin/main. - The policy migration actually reached production: /api/health/db reports {"status":"ok","connected":true,"migrationVersion": "20260816134147_readings_rls_policies"}. I am testing applied policies, not committed ones. - CI green on 3648d7a: rls-tests (2m8s), build, migrate all pass, and rls-tests gates migrate. Noted as context only -- it runs against a local stack and is not evidence about production, which is exactly why this test exists. - No Sprint 3 residue: three migrations on origin/main, no user_id migration. CRITERION 1 -- anon key, no filter, returns zero rows rather than the table. PASS. This is the sprint's actual proof, and it also collects the deny-all check carried since Sprint 2, which had never been verified live until now. The empty-table trap: my first run returned [] against what may well have been an empty table, which proves nothing at all -- [] from a denied select and [] from an empty table are byte-identical. So I inserted a row first and re-ran the identical query. With a row that provably exists (confirmed present via criterion 2 below): GET /rest/v1/readings?select=* -> 200, body: [] GET /rest/v1/readings?select=*&limit=1000 -> 200, body: [] Prefer: count=exact, Range: 0-0 -> content-range: */0 The row count leaks nothing either -- the count itself reports 0, not "1 row you may not see". CRITERION 2 -- a reading retrieved by its own id succeeds. PASS. POST /rest/v1/rpc/get_reading_by_id {"reading_id":"f5a34950-...-2bf22a22bba9"} -> 200, body verbatim: [{"id":"f5a34950-4249-4144-a5f9-2bf22a22bba9","event_date":"1969-07-20", "event_time":"20:17:00","place_name":"GroundTruth test - Sea of Tranquility", "latitude":0.6741,"longitude":23.4733,"timezone":"UTC", "created_at":"2026-08-16T15:15:22.249886+00:00"}] A random unguessed uuid through the same RPC -> 200, body: []. No leak, no error differential that would distinguish "exists but hidden" from "does not exist". I ALSO RAN THE TEST THAT DISTINGUISHES THE REAL DESIGN FROM A PLAUSIBLE WRONG ONE. A `using (true)` select policy -- the obvious-looking way to write "readable by id" -- would satisfy criterion 2 while silently failing criterion 1 on any non-empty table, and would pass criterion 1 undetected for as long as the table happened to be empty. So: GET /rest/v1/readings?id=eq.f5a34950-... -> 200, body: [] Filtered select by the correct, known id returns nothing. There is genuinely no select policy on the table; retrieval exists only through the security definer function. The design is what the migration says it is. CRITERION 3 -- update or delete of an existing reading with the anon key is refused. PASS on substance. Read the finding below on what "refused" looks like on the wire, because it is not what you would expect. PATCH /rest/v1/readings?id=eq. -> 204 PATCH /rest/v1/readings?place_name=neq.__nope__ -> 204 (mass-tamper attempt) DELETE /rest/v1/readings?id=eq. -> 204 I did not trust those status codes. Re-read the row afterwards through the RPC: it is still present, and place_name is still "GroundTruth test - Sea of Tranquility", not "TAMPERED BY GROUNDTRUTH" or "MASS TAMPER". Nothing was updated, nothing was deleted. The data is protected. FINDINGS 1. UPDATE AND DELETE FAIL SILENTLY, WITH A SUCCESS-SHAPED STATUS CODE. Severity: low for security, real for Sprint 10. All three tamper attempts returned 204 No Content, which a client reads as success. This is correct RLS behaviour -- with no update or delete policy the rows are invisible to those statements, so zero rows match and PostgREST reports "done" -- but it means the API never says no. A delete button wired straight to the Data API in Sprint 10 would appear to work every time and silently do nothing. Whoever builds that UI needs to verify by re-reading, not by checking the status code. Not a criterion failure: the criterion protects the data, and the data is protected. 2. INSERT WITH `Prefer: return=representation` IS REJECTED. Severity: will block Sprint 10 if unnoticed. POST /rest/v1/readings with Prefer: return=representation -> 401, body: {"code":"42501","message":"new row violates row-level security policy for table \"readings\""} The insert is rolled back; nothing is written. The same insert with `Prefer: return=minimal` -> 201 Created. The cause is that returning the representation requires reading the row back, and there is no select policy to permit that. The error message is actively misleading -- it blames the insert's WITH CHECK, which passed fine. Sprint 10 persists readings and will need the new row's id immediately in order to build its link. `.insert().select()` in supabase-js is the natural way to write that and it will fail with this message. The workarounds are to generate the uuid client-side and insert with return=minimal (what I did here), or to add an insert RPC that returns the id. Worth deciding before Sprint 10 rather than during it. 3. MY TEST ROW IS PERMANENTLY IN PRODUCTION AND I CANNOT REMOVE IT. id f5a34950-4249-4144-a5f9-2bf22a22bba9, place_name "GroundTruth test - Sea of Tranquility". The policy model permits anon insert and denies anon delete, so the act of proving criterion 1 honestly -- which requires a row to exist -- leaves a row behind that only the service role can clear. Someone should delete it, and should expect one more each time this sprint is re-tested. The wider point, which the sprint file already names as a deliberate decision under Out of Scope: there is no anon-reachable cleanup path at all, so anything the public inserts is permanent. That is the same surface as the rate-limiting question, and it is now demonstrated rather than theoretical. 4. THE API ACCEPTS A CLIENT-SUPPLIED id. Severity: informational. I inserted with an id I chose, which succeeded. R3 requires ids to be unguessable, and the column default is gen_random_uuid(), but nothing stops a caller from supplying a trivially guessable id for a row it creates. This is not an enumeration risk against anyone else's rows -- the attacker only controls ids for rows it inserts itself -- so it does not undermine the access model. Recording it for completeness, and to be explicit that because I supplied the id, this test does NOT exercise or prove the gen_random_uuid() default path. ADDITIONAL CHECK BEYOND THE THREE CRITERIA POST /rest/v1/rpc/tables_without_rls -> 200, body: [] Every table in the public schema has row level security enabled, verified live on production rather than from R5's test running against a local stack. LIMIT OF THIS TEST, STATED PLAINLY I verified that MY row survived the mass-update attempt.
